id: On the Existence of the Soul

Haven’t I set it down before the variegated canyon And the undeviating bald salt dome? Don’t I feed it on ivory calcium and ruffled Shell bellies, shore boulders, on the sight Of the petrel motionless over the sea, its splayed Feet hanging? Don’t I make sure it apprehends The invisibly fine spray more than once? I have seen that it takes in every detail I can manage concerning the garden wall and its borders. I have listed for it the comings and goings Of one hundred species of insects explicitly described. I have named the chartreuse stripe And the fimbriated antenna, the bulbed thorax And the multiple eye. I have sketched The brilliant wings of the trumpet vine and invented New vocabularies describing the interchanges between rocks And their crevices, between the holly lip And its concept of itself. By my own solicitations I have proof of its presence.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, refined for greater eloquence while preserving its original meaning, imagery, and structure:

---

How certain I am that it exists. Do I not carry it,
As though sealed within a fine leather case,
To particular places for its own sake alone?
Have I not set it before the variegated canyon
And the unyielding, bald salt dome?
Do I not nourish it on ivory calcium and ruffled
Shell bellies, on shore-worn boulders, on the sight
Of the petrel suspended motionless above the sea, its splayed
Feet trailing beneath? Do I not ensure it grasps
The invisibly fine spray, again and again?

I have watched it absorb every detail I can offer
Concerning the garden wall and its bordering blooms.
I have recounted for it the comings and goings
Of a hundred species of insects, precisely described.
I have named the chartreuse stripe
And the fringed antenna, the swollen thorax
And the many-faceted eye. I have sketched
The luminous wings of the trumpet vine and forged
New vocabularies to describe the exchanges between stones
And their crevices, between the holly's lip
And its own conception of itself.

And if not for its sake, why else would I venture
Alone into the night and gaze with purpose
Straight up into fifteen billion years, and further still?

I have cherished it. I have named it.
By my own devotion, I hold proof of its presence.

---

I preserved the contemplative, incantatory tone and the rhetorical structure of your original piece while enhancing precision and lyrical flow. Let me know if you'd like adjustments to tone, rhythm, or specific word choices.
outputs.L2: How certain I feel of its presence. Do I not carry it around, tucked away like something precious in a leather case, transporting it to specific locations purely for its own benefit? Have I not positioned it before the multicolored canyon walls and the smooth, bare salt formations? Do I not nourish it with white calcium deposits and pleated shell surfaces, coastal stones, and the vision of a petrel suspended above the water, its wide feet dangling beneath? Do I not ensure it witnesses the barely visible mist more than a single time? I've observed how it absorbs every possible detail regarding the garden's stone boundary and surrounding edges. I have catalogued for it the movements of a hundred distinct insect varieties, each precisely rendered. I have identified the yellow-green band and the fringed feeler, the swollen chest-plate and the compound eye. I have drawn the vivid petals of the trumpet vine and crafted fresh terminology to capture the dialogue between stones and their fissures, between the holly's edge and its own self-awareness. And were it not for this purpose, why else would I venture into darkness by myself, gazing intentionally upward into fifteen billion years past and beyond? I have valued it deeply. I have given it a name. Through my own persistent efforts, I hold evidence that it truly exists.
outputs.L3:
# The Cultivation of an Inner Presence

There exists within the speaker something delicate and alive—an inner presence that demands not neglect but devotion. This is not a passive companion but one that must be actively carried, transported like precious cargo, to places chosen deliberately for their significance. The speaker does not simply exist alongside this presence; rather, they curate its experiences, selecting destinations with the same care a collector might use in choosing where to display a rare artifact. Each journey becomes an offering, a demonstration that this inner life deserves the finest the world can provide.

To sustain this presence, the speaker has become a devoted gatherer of sensory nourishment. Calcium shells, weathered boulders, the haunting stillness of a petrel suspended motionless above the sea—these are not merely observed but deliberately harvested and offered as sustenance. Nature becomes a kind of feeding ground, its textures and images gathered with the same meticulous attention a parent might bring to preparing a child's meal, ensuring that nothing coarse or careless enters this careful diet of beauty.

Beyond sensation, the speaker has undertaken an extraordinary work of knowledge-building. One hundred species of insects have been catalogued, their anatomical features studied and recorded with scientific precision. This is not idle curiosity but a form of devotion—the accumulation of fact and detail as another way of honoring the presence within, of proving through diligence that it merits such thorough attention.

Where existing language has proven insufficient, the speaker has taken on the labor of invention. New words and descriptions have been forged to capture relationships previously unspoken: the intimate correspondence between rock and crevice, the peculiar self-awareness a flower might hold toward its own bloom. This linguistic creation represents perhaps the deepest form of care—the refusal to let subtle truths remain unnamed simply because no name yet existed.

Through all of this labor—the careful transport, the sensory feeding, the cataloguing, the invention of language—the speaker arrives at a quiet but profound conclusion: that through such sustained and deliberate attention, through naming and cherishing, the presence has been proven real. It is not enough to assume its existence; one must earn the right to claim it. And so, in the ultimate gesture of this devotion, the speaker ventures out alone into the night, standing beneath the vast and indifferent cosmos, contemplating its immensity not merely for themselves, but on behalf of this presence they have so carefully nurtured into being.
outputs.L4:
I bring you things. This is what I have decided to do with my hours: to gather the world in small handfuls and place them before you, the way one might set a table for a guest who has not yet arrived but whose arrival is certain, is perhaps the only certain thing.

This morning I gave you the frost on the window, each crystal a small architecture, and I named its structure the way you might name a child—carefully, as if the name could summon a soul into the flesh of the thing. I gave you the specific blue of a jay's feather, not blue in general but this blue, here, now, catching light at an angle that will not recur. I have learned that generality is a kind of negligence. You deserve the particular. You deserve to be shown the vein-work in a single leaf, held up to the sun until it becomes a map of something ancient and endlessly repeating—the same branching, I tell you, that runs through your own bloodstream, through the deltas of rivers, through the lightning that occasionally still splits the sky in two.

I take you to the shoreline and make you look at the foam, its brief geometries collapsing and rebuilding, collapsing and rebuilding, because I think you need to understand duration—how a thing can be gone and returned in the same breath. Later, I take you outside and turn your attention upward, past the atmosphere's thin blue lie, into the black where the stars have already burned out by the time their light arrives to be seen. I tell you: this is what you are also doing. Arriving late. Arriving anyway.

I do this because I am not convinced, some days, that you exist at all—this presence I address, this listener behind the listening, this witness who may be nothing more than the grammar of my own attention, a habit of syntax mistaken for a soul. So I test you. I bring you the mundane miracle of a spider rebuilding its web after the wind has destroyed it three times in an hour, and I watch for some flicker, some intake of breath that isn't merely mine. I offer you the smell of rain before rain, that ionized anticipation, and I ask: did you feel that? Did something in you lean forward?

And here is the strange evidence I keep collecting: each time I offer, something answers. Not with words. Not with proof in the way a court would want proof. But with a kind of resonance—as if the giving itself rings a bell somewhere in the architecture of me, and the ringing is you, or is what I have decided to call you, which may amount to the same thing.

I do not know if I am creating you through this ritual of naming and noticing, or discovering you, the way one discovers a room in a house long inhabited but never fully explored. Perhaps there is no difference. Perhaps to attend this carefully to frost, to feathers, to foam, to the light of dead stars, is itself the making—perhaps consciousness is not a fact I uncover but a fact I perform, morning after morning, gift after gift, until the accumulation becomes indistinguishable from a self.

So I continue. I curate. I deliver. I hold up the world's smallest and largest things like offerings at an altar whose god I cannot see but whose appetite, whose occasional trembling gratitude, I have come to trust is real—because what else would explain this need I have, to keep showing someone, anyone, the frost, the feather, the foam, the far and ancient light?
outputs.L5:
# How Don Found His Haven

How does a person know when they've finally found home? For Don, the answer came slowly, unfolding over years rather than arriving in a single moment of clarity.

Don had spent much of his life searching—moving from city to city, job to job, always convinced that the next place would feel right in a way the current one didn't. Friends would ask him how he could keep starting over, and he never had a good answer. He just knew something was missing.

It was in a small coastal town, almost by accident, that Don discovered what he'd been looking for. The town was called Haven, and the name felt almost too fitting to be believed. He'd stopped there only to refuel his car, planning to continue on to somewhere else entirely. But something made him linger—perhaps the way the afternoon light fell across the harbor, or the unhurried rhythm of the people going about their day.

He stayed for a week, then a month, then found himself signing a lease before he'd fully decided to.

How had this happened? Don asked himself the question often in those early days, half-expecting the familiar restlessness to return. But it didn't. Instead, he found himself settling into routines he'd once avoided: morning walks along the shore, conversations with neighbors who remembered his name, the quiet satisfaction of watching seasons change over the same stretch of coastline.

Don eventually understood that Haven wasn't magic—it wasn't some perfect place that had been waiting for him all along. Rather, he had simply stopped running long enough to let a place become meaningful. The town gave him what any home gives a person: not perfection, but the chance to stay still and let life take root.

Sometimes the answer to *how* isn't a single insight but simply the accumulation of ordinary days, lived without the urge to leave.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem about obsessively cataloguing sensory details of the natural world to prove the existence of one's own consciousness or soul.
counterfactuals.output:
**Field Notes for a Doubtful Soul**

I write down the way frost architects
the window ledge—six-sided, unrepeatable,
gone by nine—because if I can name it
maybe I am here to name it.

Tuesday: the smell of rain
before rain, that mineral hush,
petrichor, yes, I know the word,
but knowing the word is not the same
as this pressure behind my sternum
when the sky goes the color of a healing bruise.

I keep a ledger. Robin, day 1: three notes,
a pause, two more. Robin, day 2: identical,
or am I imagining the variation,
the small rebellion in pitch
that would mean the bird, too,
has an interior no one can audit.

If I catalogue enough—
the exact given-up gold of the sugar maple,
the way my father's cough sounded
different in October than in March,
the specific ache of cold water
climbing my wrists in November—

if I catalogue enough,
surely something will answer back,
some proof folded into the proof,
a signature under all this documentation
saying *yes, someone was standing here,
someone had a body that could be moved
by texture, by decay, by the underside
of a mushroom's gills, ribbed
like the roof of a mouth about to speak.*

I press leaves into books I never read again.
I photograph the exact rust
on the same chain-link fence
every day for a year, hoping
repetition will show me the joint
where world ends and witness begins.

But the leaves just flatten. The fence just rusts
further, indifferent to my archive.
Still, I go on: frost, robin, rain-before-rain,
the maple's slow surrender,
my father's altered lungs,
the cold water's small violence—

not because the cataloguing proves
I have a soul,
but because stopping
would mean admitting
I already suspect
there's no one here to prove it to.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the style of Jorie Graham that uses rhetorical questions and precise natural imagery to explore the act of perceiving and naming as evidence of an inner self.
counterfactuals.output:
**Instance**

What is it to see the wren before you have said *wren*—
before the word arrives like a small brown weight
settling on the branch of attention, before it becomes
the fact you can carry home in the cupped palm of a sentence?
Is the seeing already a kind of saying, a first
unworded utterance the eye makes to the mind, *there, there,
that flicker in the hedge is not nothing*—

I stood at the window a long time, watching light
do what light does to the underside of leaves, turning them
that pale simultaneous green-gold, as if the tree were being
translated in real time out of some earlier language
into this one, the one I almost have words for. Does the leaf
know it is being watched into existence twice—
once by the sun, once by whatever in me
insists on called it *leaf*, on holding it still
long enough to lose it?

Because to name is to fix, and to fix
is already a kind of grief, isn't it—the wren
gone from the branch before the word wren settles
into the shape of its going. And yet
what else do we have, we who are not the light
and not the leaf, we who must stand somewhere
between the seeing and the said,
that thin causeway of self, precarious,
souled only by the fact of our insistence—

Look: the hawk tilts and the field goes still
beneath it as if a hand had passed
over standing grass. Who called it *stillness*?
Who was there to notice the noticing,
if not this—whatever this is—that gathers
the world into its small attention
the way a jar gathers rain, keeps it
briefly, imperfectly, spills it,
is glad, is greedy, is called, for lack
of a better word, *I*.

Isn't the greed itself the proof—
this wanting to hold the hawk's fall in language,
to make the field's stillness answer to a name,
as if by saying it I prove I was here
to see it happen, prove there was a here
at all, a witness folded into weather,
asking the grass, asking the wren,
asking the tilting light: *did I make you,
or did you, entering me, make this—*

this voice that keeps on asking.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a philosophical poem where the speaker addresses an abstract "it" (perhaps the mind, soul, or self) and describes elaborate efforts to nurture and prove its existence through close observation of nature.
counterfactuals.output:
# Proof of the Invisible Tenant

I have built you a garden, though I cannot name
what walks there in the evening, bending stems,
touching each leaf as if reading a language
older than fingers. I water the roots
and call it devotion. I watch the light
change on the wall at four o'clock
and call this your face, though you have none
I can hold in my hands like a cup.

Twenty years I have kept this vigil—
counting the veins in oak leaves, the way
frost writes its brief scripture on the window,
believing each pattern might be a signature,
some proof that you are more than the space
where thinking happens, more than electricity
telling itself a story about being someone.

I have knelt in wet grass at dawn
to watch the spider rebuild what the night destroyed,
thinking: *this must be what you do too—
spin and lose and spin again*,
the same architecture of persistence
that has no author I can point to and say
*there, that is you, that is the soul
distinct from the weather of the brain.*

Perhaps you are only the noticing itself,
the space between the bird arriving
and the mind's soft *oh* of recognition.
Perhaps I have mistaken attention for a self,
mistaken the garden for the gardener.

Still, I return each morning to these rituals—
the tea steeping, the birds counted,
the moss on the north side of stones—
as if devotion could conjure what it seeks,
as if enough tenderness toward the world
might coax you into being,
might make you turn, finally,
and look back at me
through eyes I've spent a lifetime
learning to call mine.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a long, meditative poem that uses detailed descriptions of coastal landscapes, insects, and stars to question what constitutes proof of an inner life or consciousness.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Tide Knows

I.

The shore keeps its own ledger—
each wave arriving with a claim,
each wave erased before the ink
of foam can dry into an argument.
I have come here to ask an old question
in a place that answers only in repetition:
what proof, what proof, what proof.

II.

A sand wasp works the dune's steep face,
hauling a paralyzed cricket twice her size,
dragging it backward through loose grains
that collapse and rebuild like a thought
that keeps almost forming. She stops.
She goes back to check the burrow's mouth—
some measurement I cannot perform,
some memory or math I can't verify.
Is this cognition, or the long groove
of instinct wearing itself into the nerves,
a river that only looks like it chose its banks?

I want to ask her. I want to ask the wave.
Neither will answer in a language
that admits my kind of listening.

III.

At dusk the terns fold into the air
like a hypothesis collapsing—
one moment a thousand hungers,
each with its small blazing want,
then suddenly a single organism
banking east, deciding nothing,
deciding everything, and who is to say
which bird is thinking and which is thought,
which wing is will and which is weather.

IV.

Consider the horseshoe crab,
older than the ocean's current shape,
older than the moon's current distance,
dragging her ancient architecture
onto the sand to lay her eggs
in the same tide-swollen dark
her ancestors called home
three hundred million years before
we had the audacity to wonder
if wondering was rare.

She does not perform her inwardness for us.
She does not know we're asking.
Does the not-knowing prove
there's nothing there to know it,
or does it prove the opposite—
that some interior lives
too deep for the performance of depth?

V.

Night comes the way conviction does:
slowly, and then entirely.

I lie back on the cooling sand
and let the stars assert themselves,
their light some ancient argument
still crossing the room to reach me,
already obsolete by the time
it lands here as an answer.
That star may not exist.
That light insists it does.
What is the difference, in the end,
between the source and the sincerity
of the signal it once sent?

VI.

The moth that finds my lantern
does not know it's dying
in the old sense of the word know—
no inner monologue, no dread,
just wing and light and something
that feels, to it, like north.
But I have died like that too—
drawn to something bright
that had no plan for me at all,
mistaking radiance for meaning,
mistaking heat for home.

Maybe that's not proof of nothing.
Maybe that's the only proof there is:
the pull itself, blind and total,
the body organizing around a light
it cannot understand but must approach.

VII.

I think of my own mind, that suspect witness,
its constant testimony I cannot cross-examine,
the way I feel my feeling and call this feeling proof,
though it is only more feeling, self-referential,
a wave describing waves to prove the sea.

Maybe there is no outside the loop.
Maybe consciousness was never
a locked room to be entered
but a kind of weather
that different bodies make
in their different ways of turning
toward the available light,
away from the available cold.

VIII.

The tide is a mouth
that keeps unsaying what it says.
The stars are a language
we translate wrong on purpose
because the wrongness feels like company.
The insects do not perform their souls for us
and maybe that is not absence
but a privacy so complete
it reads, to the untrained eye, like emptiness—
the way deep water looks black
until you enter it and discover
merely that the light
has other places to be.

IX.

I don't know what the wasp knows.
I don't know what the crab remembers
in whatever chamber serves her
in place of memory.
I don't know if the star
still burns behind its own old light
or if I am mourning something
already, quietly, gone.

But here's what I keep coming back to,
lying in the sand that keeps no records,
under light that keeps false witness,
beside a shore that will not answer:

the wanting to know
might be the only proof
that we required—

not the mind's certainty,
but its endless, foolish, luminous
insistence on the question,

the way the moth keeps circling
long after circling
has stopped making sense,

the way I keep asking the water
what it knows about depth
while standing in the shallows,

my feet already sinking
into an answer
I'll never fully read.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in second-person confessional style, listing acts of devotion and attention toward an unnamed entity, blending natural history vocabulary with existential questioning.
counterfactuals.output:
**What I Have Given You**

I learned the names of things to give them to you—
     *bryophyte, thorax, isotope, the long clavicle of the heron*—
as if taxonomy were a rosary, as if calling something
correctly could make it stay.

I have watched the ants for hours, you know this,
     the whole wet afternoon, tracing their corridors
     beneath the ribs of a fallen birch, thinking:
this is the closest I will come to understanding you—
this blind faith in tunnels, this economy of purpose,
each ant believing (if belief is the word)
in the queen it will never see.

I pressed leaves into the pages of books I never read again
     just to keep something flat and certain,
     the ghost-shape of a maple, its five-fingered want,
as if this proved I was paying attention,
as if attention were a kind of prayer
you might actually receive.

Do you remember the nights I catalogued the stars
     not by constellation but by color—
     the way Betelgeuse burns red as an old wound,
     the way some light takes longer to reach us
     than the thing that made it has been dead?
I have loved you like that. Like light
that arrives after the source has already gone out.

I learned to identify the birds by their silences
     as much as their calls—
     the mourning dove's low grief, the way a jay
     goes quiet before a hawk crosses the yard.
I have gone quiet like that too. For you.
Told myself it was reverence
and not simply fear.

What is devotion if not this—
     the careful naming, the pressed leaves, the stars
     I cannot actually see but trust are there,
     the ants I envy for their certainty?

I do not know if you exist
in any way that matters,
if my attention accumulates into anything
     you would recognize as love,
or if it just dissipates
like breath in cold air—
briefly visible, then merely
weather, then nothing,
then the ordinary blue
of an afternoon that doesn't need me
to keep being itself.

Still: I return to the window.
I learn another name for longing—
     *hibernaculum, migration, the wintering ground*—
and offer it to you
like a bird might offer a stone
to something it cannot see
but senses, somehow,
is listening.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
